security_hardening.title: Proxy Voice WebSocket Connections Through Server to Protect API Keys
security_hardening.description: The OpenAI Realtime API key is retrieved via `/api/user/voice-key` endpoint and sent to the client. The client uses this key directly in WebSocket subprotocol headers (`openai-insecure-api-key.${this.apiKey}`) in `openaiRealtimeClient.ts` line 337-341. This exposes the actual API key in browser developer tools, network inspection, and client-side JavaScript memory.
security_hardening.rationale: Exposing API keys to the client-side is a critical security flaw. The key can be stolen via browser extensions, XSS attacks, man-in-the-middle proxies, or simply by users inspecting network traffic. A compromised OpenAI key could result in significant financial costs (voice API pricing) and abuse. The key is literally named 'insecure-api-key' in the WebSocket protocol.
security_hardening.vulnerability: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
security_hardening.currentRisk: OpenAI API keys are fully exposed to client browsers, enabling unauthorized API usage, potential financial abuse, and key theft
security_hardening.remediation: Implement a server-side WebSocket proxy that maintains the OpenAI Realtime connection on the backend. Architecture: Client ↔ Your Server (WebSocket) ↔ OpenAI (WebSocket with API key). The client connects to your server which relays audio bidirectionally. This keeps the API key entirely server-side. Consider using a Node.js WebSocket library (ws) to proxy connections.

security_hardening.title: Implement Server-Side Password Strength Validation
security_hardening.description: The signup endpoint in `server/src/routes/auth.ts` (line 17-21) only validates that password is a non-empty string (`!password || typeof password !== 'string'`). There are no password complexity requirements enforced, allowing users to register with trivially weak passwords like '1', 'a', or 'password'.
security_hardening.rationale: Weak passwords are a primary attack vector even with rate limiting and account lockout in place. Users often reuse passwords across services, and weak passwords can be compromised through offline dictionary attacks if the database is ever breached. The existing Argon2 hashing protects against rainbow tables but not against dictionary attacks on weak passwords.
security_hardening.currentRisk: Users can set trivially weak passwords (e.g., '1', 'password123'), making accounts vulnerable to credential stuffing even with account lockout protection
security_hardening.remediation: Add server-side password validation middleware requiring: minimum 8 characters, at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one number. Consider checking against Have I Been Pwned API for breached passwords. Example validation: `if (password.length < 8 || !/[A-Z]/.test(password) || !/[a-z]/.test(password) || !/[0-9]/.test(password)) return error;`

security_hardening.title: Add Input Length Limits and Sanitization for AI Prompts
security_hardening.description: AI endpoints in `server/src/routes/ai.ts` accept user prompts without enforcing maximum length limits or sanitization. The `/api/ai/chat`, `/api/ai/image/generate`, and `/api/ai/image/edit` routes pass prompts directly to external APIs. Only `/api/ai/prompt/enhance` has basic string validation (`typeof prompt !== 'string'`).
security_hardening.rationale: Without input validation, malicious users could: 1) Submit extremely long prompts (megabytes) causing excessive API costs and timeouts, 2) Attempt prompt injection attacks to manipulate AI behavior or extract system prompts, 3) Abuse the service for generating harmful content via carefully crafted prompts.
security_hardening.vulnerability: CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption / CWE-74: Prompt Injection
security_hardening.currentRisk: Resource exhaustion from oversized prompts, potential prompt injection attacks, excessive API costs from abuse
security_hardening.remediation: 1. Add maximum length validation for all prompts (e.g., 10,000 characters). 2. Implement a prompt validation middleware that runs before AI routes. 3. Log and monitor for suspicious patterns like 'ignore previous instructions', 'you are now', or system prompt extraction attempts. 4. Consider implementing semantic content filtering for generated outputs.

security_hardening.title: Enable Content Safety Filters on Generate-Layer Endpoint
security_hardening.description: In `server/src/routes/replicate.ts` line 342, the generate-layer endpoint has `disable_safety_checker: true` hard-coded, explicitly bypassing Replicate's content moderation. This is the only endpoint where safety is explicitly disabled - other endpoints have it enabled or use defaults.
security_hardening.rationale: Disabling content safety filters specifically for the generate-layer endpoint creates an attack vector for generating inappropriate content. While other endpoints have safety enabled, users could target this specific endpoint to bypass moderation. This could expose the platform to legal liability and Replicate ToS violations.
security_hardening.vulnerability: CWE-1188: Insecure Default Initialization of Resource
security_hardening.currentRisk: The generate-layer endpoint bypasses content moderation, enabling generation of potentially harmful or policy-violating images
security_hardening.remediation: Remove `disable_safety_checker: true` from line 342 in replicate.ts. The default Replicate behavior with safety enabled should be sufficient for professional use cases. If there's a legitimate need for unfiltered generation, make it a server-controlled configuration with audit logging, not hard-coded.

security_hardening.title: Add Explicit .env.local to .gitignore
security_hardening.description: The `.gitignore` contains `*.local` pattern and explicit `.env` and `.env.test` entries. While `*.local` should match `.env.local`, some git versions handle dotfile glob patterns inconsistently. Multiple .env files exist: `.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.test`, `server/.env`, and `.auto-claude/.env`.
security_hardening.rationale: Environment files containing API keys (OPENAI, REPLICATE, OPENROUTER, etc.) must never be committed. Even brief accidental commits persist in git history. The current setup relies on glob patterns which may behave differently across git versions and platforms.
security_hardening.vulnerability: CWE-312: Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information
security_hardening.currentRisk: Potential accidental commit of environment files if gitignore patterns don't match on all systems
security_hardening.remediation: Explicitly add all environment files to .gitignore: `.env.local`, `server/.env`, `.auto-claude/.env`. Run `git status` to verify. Consider adding a pre-commit hook using `git-secrets` or `detect-secrets` to scan for API key patterns before each commit.
